British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

First Nations leaders in Alberta say ballot shortages, late-opening polling stations and identification rules obstructed some Indigenous voters during Monday’s provincial referendum. The nonbinding vote asked whether Alberta should begin legal steps toward a future separation referendum; about three-quarters of voters chose to remain in Canada, and Premier Danielle Smith said she would not call another separation vote while she is premier [aptnnews.ca#1][cbc.ca#5][thestar.com#1]. Treaty 8 campaign manager Jay Telegdi said he received reports of voters turned away because of identification and polling problems. Elections Alberta said it delivered extra ballots to five First Nations communities, three of which received multiple deliveries. The agency said 36 First Nations communities participated, up from 33 in 2023 [cbc.ca#5][theglobeandmail.com#11]. Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot called for changes to prevent similar barriers in future elections [aptnnews.ca#3]. The count on the nine other ballot questions remained unsettled Tuesday. Preliminary results showed support for all five immigration proposals and close contests on constitutional measures; Smith said she would pursue immigration reforms in the months and years ahead. Elections Alberta scheduled the official results for Oct. 29 [lethbridgeherald.com#3][timescolonist.com#2][cbc.ca#3].

items.title: [zmescience.com] Protein evidence identifies Chinese fossils as Denisovans, revealing likely facial traits
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.

items.title: [MacRumors] Apple Ordered to Open iPhone to Rival App Stores in Australia
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Australia's Federal Court today ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads, and alternative payment services for Australian users from March 1, 2027.


The orders follow the court's August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by restricting app distribution and payment options. They cover users whose Apple Account region is Australia, with Apple Developer Program members worldwide able to participate.

Apple must let users find, download, install, and update apps through competing marketplaces and websites without charging for access or obstructing their use. Developers must receive the necessary tools on substantially the same terms as for App Store distribution, and Apple cannot penalize them for using competing stores or payment services.

Developers will also be able to offer alternative payments and link to other ways to pay, including within ‌App Store‌ apps. Apple cannot require them to offer its own purchasing system alongside alternatives, report those transactions, or allow Apple to audit them. Developers can offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple preventing them.

The ruling also limits Apple's ability to collect fees on those purchases. It cannot charge for purchases through alternative payment services or websites in apps distributed outside the ‌App Store‌. For ‌App Store‌ apps, fees are capped at the equivalent charge for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine, reasonable additional costs Apple incurs for digital purchases.

Apple also cannot make alternative distribution conditional on developers offering content purchased elsewhere through its own payment system.

Security checks will remain. Apps downloaded outside the ‌App Store‌ must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and be notarized by Apple or a qualified third party. However, Apple cannot impose disproportionate installation barriers or otherwise obstruct alternative distribution. Additional security requirements for competing payments must be necessary and proportionate, with developers given an explanation in advance.

Apple can remove or disable externally installed apps only in specified cases involving harmful content, genuine security risks, or legal requirements. It cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones, but does not have to distribute competing stores through the ‌App Store‌.

Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and ‌App Store‌ security.

The changes take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for a court-approved extension until May 3.

items.title: [Fast Company] Consuming political news can hurt your job performance
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

With the midterm elections around the corner, political anxiety is in season—and productivity could pay the price.

A new study from researchers at Texas A&M University shows that consuming political news and social media outside of work affects employees’ emotional states and workplace behavior, even if they aren’t discussing politics at the water cooler.

Researchers tracked more than 300 workers over nine weeks during the 2024 presidential primary season, asking them to report how often they consumed political information, whether they viewed it as positive or negative, and how engaged, anxious, hopeful, and helpful they felt at work.

During weeks when workers consumed political information that they perceived as negative, they tended to report higher anxiety and lower engagement. During weeks when they consumed more political news that they saw as positive, they reported stronger engagement and greater willingness to help coworkers.

The takeaway is that the broader political environment affects the workplace even when politics aren’t directly discussed at the office. 

“Political information is designed to capture attention and provoke emotional reactions,” the study’s lead author, Ian Hughes, an assistant professor of psychological and brain sciences, said in a statement. “Those reactions don’t necessarily disappear once people close an app or turn off the TV.”

Organizations should be aware that employees are often dealing with additional stress during election season, he added.

“Political information has emotional consequences,” he said. “Those emotions can affect other parts of life, and that includes work.”

The study recommends that organizations provide mental health resources and support for stress management. Managers can reduce political stress by providing time off for voting or encouraging volunteering, which can increase employees’ sense of agency and control.

Workers should also engage in leisure and recovery activities, pursue “resource-building” practices such as mindfulness, gratitude, and sleep, and take breaks from media consumption.

PHP maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for the two flaws, which had remained hidden for years and could let attackers run code on vulnerable servers without authentication. The same capabilities could help attackers adapt exploits to different PHP versions and server configurations, the company warned. It is proposing a repeatable process for identifying and fixing vulnerabilities in widely used software and preparing defenses against them. Thousands of people demonstrated across Italy on Saturday, Oct. 24, against rising living costs and war. Police and protesters clashed in Rome, Turin and Bologna, while the Milan march was largely peaceful. Police used tear gas and water cannons in several cities. Authorities said nine people were arrested and 371 were temporarily detained in eight cities, including 110 minors. Demonstrators raised concerns about housing and fuel costs, wages, public services and military spending. Security measures followed the previous weekend’s looting and clashes in Milan, where shops in the fashion district boarded up windows as a precaution. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government sent 500 additional soldiers to Milan and approved tougher measures involving minors. On Saturday, police also detained 30-year-old freelance journalist Youssef Siher, suspected of organizing the 17 October Movement. They searched more than 150 locations in Milan, Monza and about 20 other cities as part of investigations into the earlier unrest.

items.title: [koaa.com] U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot. The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. UNEP says a pathway offering about a 50% chance of limiting peak warming to 1.7–1.8°C and returning to 1.5°C by 2100 requires global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

items.title: [phys.org] Full-scale wave test shows salt marshes can buffer coastal storms
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers moved 306 square meters of intact salt marsh into the Delta Flume, a large wave-testing facility in Delft, Netherlands, and exposed it to waves as high as 2 meters. After 21 hours, the marsh surface had eroded by an average of just 7 millimeters, while its vegetation suffered progressive damage. The study found that plants can reduce wave energy by more than 10%, and by as much as 50% on lower-energy coasts with waves up to 1 meter. Their effect declines as waves grow higher and vegetation is lost. Researchers say marshes could work alongside dikes and seawalls, not replace them. A Spanish coastal-engineering expert questioned how well the Dutch experiment applies to other coastlines, citing wave periods and mobile seabeds among other factors.
